section_summary: This section centers on wartime controls over strategic materials and public criticism of prewar U.S. exports to Japan, including mercury, scrap iron, aircraft, copper, machine tools, and a supposed tracer-bullet formula. It contains correspondence with citizens and members of Congress, internal policy memoranda, and diplomatic reporting from Mexico, Chile, Argentina, Switzerland, Britain, Sweden, and China. The final documents describe extensive leakage of wool, cotton, tung oil, bristles, and wolfram from unoccupied China into Japanese-controlled territory.

subfiles.title: Messersmith to Bateman on rumors of mercury smuggling from Mexico
subfiles.about: Messersmith assesses reports that Mexican mercury was being smuggled to enemy destinations.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith considers small-scale smuggling across the Mexican border into the United States plausible but strategically harmless. He finds no evidence for shipment by German submarines, while acknowledging that possible exports to Argentina merit investigation. He stresses Mexican cooperation and refers Bateman to earlier confidential reports and to Ransom and Bonsal.

subfiles.title: Departmental reply concerning A. Z. Phillips and continuing mercury reports
subfiles.about: The writer disputes Phillips's claim that he ceased Japanese shipments when they became illegal and explains the request for a fresh mercury report.
subfiles.summary: State links A. Z. Phillips to an October 1941 mercury-smuggling case found by Vice Consul Hoyt at Manzanillo; Grew's activities were regarded as closed, but recurring reports prompted the inquiry to Ransom.

subfiles.title: Johnson to Hull forwarding Vincent's inquiry
subfiles.about: Johnson forwards a constituent's letter about alleged treaty obligations governing scrap-metal sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Representative Johnson sends Hull W. P. Vincent's letter, asks State to answer him directly with a copy, and requests the enclosure's return.

subfiles.title: Vincent to Johnson asking about a supposed 1920 trade agreement
subfiles.about: Vincent asks whether a Harding-era agreement compelled the United States to sell scrap metal to Japan until 1941.
subfiles.summary: Vincent reports partisan controversy over scrap sales to Japan and asks Johnson to confirm a supposed 1920 agreement exchanging American commodities for Japanese silk over twenty-one years.

subfiles.title: Duplicate of Vincent's inquiry about scrap-metal trade
subfiles.about: This copy repeats Vincent's inquiry concerning a supposed twenty-one-year trade agreement with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate of Vincent's letter seeking facts to answer Republican criticism of Democratic responsibility for scrap exports.

subfiles.title: Department acknowledgment returning Vincent's letter
subfiles.about: The Department returns Vincent's letter and supplies Johnson with a copy of its answer.
subfiles.summary: State says an officer answered Vincent directly and returns the original and a copy of the response to Johnson.

subfiles.title: Atcheson to Vincent explaining the 1911 treaty and export controls
subfiles.about: Atcheson corrects Vincent's account of the treaty with Japan and summarizes the legal basis for later export restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson tells Vincent the 1911 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation, terminated in January 1940, required no sales of particular commodities; export-control authority came in June 1940, and licenses to Japan were generally denied.

subfiles.title: Memorandum reconciling aircraft-export and arms-license figures
subfiles.to: Carlton Savage and the Assistant Secretary
subfiles.about: The memorandum explains why Commerce Department aircraft-export totals exceeded State Department arms-license figures.
subfiles.summary: Commerce put aircraft and parts exported to Japan above eleven million dollars in 1938; after consulting Mr. Roberts, the writer says the gap consisted mostly of engines, instruments and parts not needing licenses under the 1937 order.

subfiles.title: Savage to Hamilton on Senator Lucas's request
subfiles.about: Savage reports Senator Lucas's request for material rebutting Representative Chiperfield's accusations about arms exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Savage tells Hamilton Senator Lucas's office asked for information; the disputed charges came from an October 12 Chicago Daily Tribune article by Chesly Manly.

subfiles.title: Memorandum submitting a draft response for Senator Lucas
subfiles.about: The memorandum submits a draft letter and supporting paper tailored to Chiperfield's reported claims.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum submits a draft reply to Senator Lucas's oral request, confining supporting material to the Chicago Tribune allegations.

subfiles.title: Acheson to Lucas transmitting a policy memorandum
subfiles.about: Acheson sends Lucas a memorandum intended to answer criticism of American arms and war-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Acheson acknowledges Lucas's oral request and encloses a detailed memorandum for use in the controversy.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on arms exports, neutrality law, and economic restrictions against Japan
subfiles.about: The memorandum reviews the legal framework, statistics, and gradual development of American economic controls on Japan from 1937 through 1941.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum distinguishes licensed arms from raw materials, explains neutrality law couldn't discriminate between China and Japan, shows licenses and exports fell after the 1938 moral embargo, and traces the 1911 treaty's end, the 1940 act and the 1941 freeze.

subfiles.title: Clinton to Hull urging removal of Japanese residents from Hawaii
subfiles.about: Clinton cites his earlier warnings about Philippine metal exports and urges the removal of Japanese residents from the Hawaiian Islands.
subfiles.summary: Clinton says his January warning about Philippine metal shipments to Japan was ignored and urges removing Japanese residents from Hawaii; the letter contains sweeping racial assertions.

subfiles.title: Hoskins's acknowledgment of Clinton's letter
subfiles.about: Hoskins acknowledges Clinton's proposals and refers the matter to the War Department.
subfiles.summary: Hoskins says the Japanese-resident question mainly belongs to the War Department, forwards Clinton's letter, and suggests he write there directly.

subfiles.title: Wright to Hull criticizing wartime leadership and prewar scrap exports
subfiles.about: Wright challenges Hull's comments about critics and condemns the government's record on scrap exports, Pearl Harbor, and the Philippines.
subfiles.summary: Wright criticizes wartime leadership, saying officials should have anticipated enemy action, citing scrap returning as Japanese shells, Pearl Harbor and the Philippines' loss.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Hull's October 27 press conference
subfiles.from: M. J. McDermott, Division of Current Information
subfiles.about: The memorandum records Hull's comments on India, Martinique, Ecuador, and the temporary informational advantage enjoyed by critics.
subfiles.summary: Hull's October 27 press conference: on India the government is watching but can't disclose diplomatic details; he expects a final Martinique statement and welcomes Ecuador's president; clarifies the remark behind Harold Wright's complaint.

subfiles.title: Department reply clarifying Hull's statement to Wright
subfiles.about: The Department explains that Hull's remark concerned the inability to disclose details of policy toward India.
subfiles.summary: State thanks Wright, summarizes the October 27 press exchange, and explains that officials handling foreign affairs can't publicly reveal all facts; the text ends before the conclusion.

subfiles.title: Duplicate acknowledgment of Clinton's letter
subfiles.about: This copy repeats the referral of Clinton's recommendations to the War Department.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate acknowledgment to Clinton: a War Department matter; his letter is forwarded and he may write there directly.

subfiles.title: Stockholm telegram reporting despatch of requested information
subfiles.about: The Stockholm mission reports that extensive requested data had already been sent by confidential despatch.
subfiles.summary: Stockholm: the figures requested in the August circular were too lengthy for telegram and went in confidential despatch 1081 of October 21, leaving October 31.

subfiles.title: London telegram concerning British economic-warfare information
subfiles.to: Secretary of State and Board of Economic Warfare
subfiles.about: The embassy reports that Britain cannot yet separate the requested data from a broader Ministry of Economic Warfare inquiry.
subfiles.summary: London: Major Harrold says the requested information is tied to a larger investigation, and he will bring it to Washington to discuss with the Board of Economic Warfare.

subfiles.title: Catch slip for an Argentina telegram
subfiles.about: The slip requests telegram no. 176 of November 19 concerning Argentina for correction at the requester's desk.
subfiles.summary: Catch slip directing records staff to bring an Argentina telegram to Marie Crawford's desk; notes a missing number.

subfiles.title: Duggan memorandum on a Japanese plan to acquire Chilean copper
subfiles.about: Duggan reports intelligence that Japan sought to route Chilean copper through Argentina using a company called de la Jera.
subfiles.summary: Duggan calls the information on a Japanese plan to acquire Chilean copper unquestionably reliable and asks that feasibility be investigated and the Buenos Aires and Santiago embassies alerted.

subfiles.title: Department telegram directing investigation of the copper scheme
subfiles.to: American Embassy, Santiago; repeated to Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: The Department instructs Santiago to investigate a reported plan for Chilean copper to be exported through Argentina to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Telegram repeats intelligence on a company styled de la Jara; Santiago is asked to judge the copper operation's feasibility and Buenos Aires gets the instruction too.

subfiles.title: Bern telegram on outstanding Japanese machine-tool orders
subfiles.about: Bern reports preliminary information on machine tools ordered from Swiss firms for Japanese customers before Japan entered the war.
subfiles.summary: A Swiss trading concern supplied a list covering about seventy machines made by fifteen firms for roughly twenty Japanese customers. Eleven machines and assorted tools were ready for delivery, while completion of the remainder ranged from one month to one year. The legation promised further information on actual shipments.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Bern telegram no. 5452
subfiles.about: This paraphrase restates Bern's preliminary findings on outstanding Swiss machine-tool orders for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase records approximately seventy specialized machines intended largely for automotive-parts manufacture. Only eleven machines and assorted gauges, hobs, grinding wheels, and vibrometers were ready, and the legation offered to telegraph manufacturer and customer details. A later report was promised on any completed shipments.

subfiles.title: Santiago telegram identifying the Delajara intermediary
subfiles.about: The embassy identifies the suspected Chilean intermediary and evaluates the first stage of the proposed copper transaction.
subfiles.summary: Santiago: Delejere is Guillermo Delajaramont of Ovalle Delajara y Cia, who sold metals to Japan's government, served as attache in Japan and returned on the Gripsholm; Bowers finds export to Argentina feasible and leaves onward shipment to Buenos Aires.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Santiago telegram no. 2078
subfiles.about: This paraphrase repeats Santiago's identification of Delajaramont and its assessment of the proposed copper route.
subfiles.summary: Paraphrase of Santiago telegram 2078: Delajaramont dealt with the Japanese government and served at the Chilean Embassy in Japan; Chilean copper could go to Argentina, and Buenos Aires should judge re-export to Japan.

subfiles.title: Hudson to Roosevelt asking whether scrap is still being sold to Japan
subfiles.about: Hudson asks whether a claim that the United States continued selling scrap to Japan was true or propaganda.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten constituent letter reports a statement heard the previous day. Hudson requests a prompt factual answer from the president.

subfiles.title: Smyth to Hudson denying continued scrap sales
subfiles.about: Smyth explains when scrap exports to Japan were restricted and when bilateral trade ceased.
subfiles.summary: Smyth tells Hudson export controls began July 1940, Japan license applications were generally denied, all scrap was denied from October 16, 1940, the July 1941 freeze nearly ended trade, and war ended it.

subfiles.title: Baptist to Welles claiming vindication of his prewar warnings
subfiles.about: Baptist sends extracts from earlier letters as evidence that he had predicted Axis cooperation and urged an embargo on scrap exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Baptist claims vindication: his forecasts of an Axis alliance and Japanese attacks came true, and he condemns scrap and war-material exports despite his appeals to Roosevelt, Hull and Congress.

subfiles.title: Compilation of Baptist's 1939–1940 letters opposing aid to Japan
subfiles.to: Clifton A. Woodrum, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Arthur H. Vandenberg, Cordell Hull, Henry L. Stimson, James F. Byrnes, Sumner Welles, and Harry F. Byrd
subfiles.about: The compilation reproduces Baptist's earlier appeals for an embargo on scrap iron and other strategic goods sent to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The excerpts denounce American exports as assistance to Japanese aggression against China and predict an alliance with Germany and Italy. Baptist warns that Japan might seize French Indochina, the Dutch East Indies, and the Philippines and eventually use American-supplied material against the United States. Other passages discuss domestic subversion, defense-industry labor, aid to Britain, and obligations under the Nine-Power Treaty.

subfiles.title: Clipping titled “Facts Embargoed Instead of Scrap”
subfiles.to: Filed with J. H. Baptist's correspondence
subfiles.about: The article criticizes continued American sales of oil, copper, machine tools, and previously scrap iron to Japan while withholding embarrassing statistics.
subfiles.summary: Clipping "Facts Embargoed Instead of Scrap": big scrap exports caused shortage and may return as shells, mocking oil sales as deterrence; Baptist notes his warnings predated it.

subfiles.title: Atcheson to Baptist reviewing economic restrictions on Japan
subfiles.about: Atcheson responds to Baptist's criticism with a chronology of American economic measures against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson cites the 1938 moral embargo, credit discouragement and the 1911 treaty's end; broad export authority came only in July 1940, after which goods were progressively controlled, and the July 1941 freeze practically ended trade.

subfiles.title: Buenos Aires telegram on possible clandestine copper transshipment
subfiles.about: Buenos Aires reports that Chilean copper might be transferred covertly to Spanish or Swedish vessels despite negligible recorded Argentine exports.
subfiles.summary: Buenos Aires: much copper enters from Chile but official figures show almost no onward exports; ship-to-ship transfers in harbor could escape statistics; Japan getting it via Spain or Sweden is doubtful but not excluded.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Buenos Aires telegram no. 2550
subfiles.about: This paraphrase repeats the embassy's assessment of unrecorded copper transshipment from Chile through Buenos Aires.
subfiles.summary: Paraphrase of Buenos Aires telegram 2550: copper arrivals contrast with negligible exports; Chilean vessels could transfer cargo to Swedish or Spanish ships unrecorded; investigation continues.

subfiles.title: Confidential instruction reporting Japanese orders to buy Chilean copper
subfiles.about: The Department relays protected intelligence that Japan's minister in Santiago had authority to purchase copper through the Delajara company.
subfiles.summary: Airmail instruction: the Japanese minister was reportedly told to act when conditions favor, settle transport, price and payment, direct Talbo, watch Chile's attitude and notify Chile to show Japan's wish to resume trade.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum requesting legal review of tracer-bullet replies
subfiles.about: The division asks the Legal Adviser's office to review draft replies concerning an allegation that State ordered a tracer-bullet formula sold to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs asks legal review of draft replies to Senator George and Representative Tarver on the tracer bullet, asking whether an earlier policy on exporting arms patents requires changing them.

subfiles.title: Tarver to Hull forwarding Cooper's tracer-bullet inquiry
subfiles.about: Tarver forwards a constituent's letter and clipping about an alleged State Department order involving a tracer-bullet secret.
subfiles.summary: Tarver asks Hull for information that may properly go to Lt. Col. Mark Cooper, who will pass it to the American Legion post in Rome, Georgia.

subfiles.title: Cooper to Tarver concerning General Hatcher
subfiles.about: Cooper asks Tarver to identify the State Department official allegedly responsible for giving a tracer-bullet formula to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cooper encloses a magazine item, respects General Hatcher, and wants an answer for the Legion post if it won't embarrass Hatcher.

subfiles.title: “General Julian Hatcher—Hero without Headlines”
subfiles.from: Magazine item quoting Drew Pearson's broadcast
subfiles.about: The item alleges that Hatcher evaded an official order to release a new tracer-bullet formula for sale to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Pearson's column says Hatcher was ordered through State to give a company his secret formula for Japan and substituted an older formula whose cartridges exploded after six months.

subfiles.title: Department reply to Senator George denying the tracer-bullet allegation
subfiles.about: Hull reports that State Department records contain no evidence of any order or communication concerning sale of Hatcher's tracer-bullet formula.
subfiles.summary: State tells Senator George a thorough search found no communication with Hatcher or anyone about transferring such a formula, and returns the news item.

subfiles.title: Senator George's tracer-bullet inquiry
subfiles.about: George quotes a constituent's request to identify the official allegedly responsible for transferring Hatcher's tracer-bullet secret to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Senator George asks State's advice on a constituent's magazine report about the tracer bullet and requests the enclosure's return.

subfiles.title: Duplicate clipping on General Julian Hatcher
subfiles.from: Magazine item quoting Drew Pearson's broadcast
subfiles.about: This copy repeats the allegation that Hatcher substituted a defective tracer-bullet formula for one ordered released to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate clipping on Hatcher defying a State order, claiming the substituted cartridges explode after six months.

subfiles.title: Hull to Tarver denying the tracer-bullet allegation
subfiles.about: Hull tells Tarver that departmental records disclose no involvement in a sale of Hatcher's tracer-bullet formula.
subfiles.summary: Hull tells Tarver State found no communication with Hatcher or anyone about selling the formula to Japanese or other interests, and returns Cooper's letter.

subfiles.title: Bern telegram listing Swiss machine tools ordered for Japanese firms
subfiles.to: Secretary of State and Board of Economic Warfare
subfiles.about: Bern supplies a detailed list of Swiss machine tools, manufacturers, and Japanese customers connected with outstanding prewar orders.
subfiles.summary: The list includes lathes, milling and grinding machines, thread grinders, jig borers, shapers, automatics, boring machines, measuring machines, and gear-hobbing equipment. It also notes assorted vibrometers, gauges, grinding wheels, and hobs for unnamed Japanese firms. The information follows the legation's November 26 preliminary report.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Bern telegram no. 6177
subfiles.about: This paraphrase reorganizes the list of Swiss machine tools and Japanese purchasers transmitted from Bern.
subfiles.summary: Each entry gives the quantity and type of machine, the Swiss manufacturer, and the Japanese customer. The equipment ranges from lathes and grinding machines to jig borers, automatics, and gear-hobbing machines. The legation says fuller details on a separate group of tools could possibly be obtained.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs comment on Chinese strategic-material leakage
subfiles.about: The memorandum considers cautious ways the United States might address Chinese trade in strategic materials with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs sees Chinese politics, weak authority and monopolies as complications in strategic-material leakage; suggests an informal approach to T. V. Soong or tactful Board of Economic Warfare action after consulting the Chongqing ambassador.

subfiles.title: Gauss despatch transmitting Service's report on Chinese trade with Japan
subfiles.about: Gauss forwards John Service's observations on the movement of Chinese strategic materials to Japanese-controlled areas.
subfiles.summary: Gauss sends Service's report: wool from Ningxia to Japanese-held Suiyuan, cotton east from Henan, tung oil and bristles reaching the Japanese, and wolfram diverted; purchasing monopolies depress producer earnings and encourage illicit sales.

subfiles.title: Service memorandum on Chinese trade in strategic materials with Japan
subfiles.about: Service analyzes how wool, cotton, tung oil, bristles, and wolfram moved from unoccupied China into Japanese hands.
subfiles.summary: Service describes wool caravans, Henan cotton smuggling and tung oil reaching occupied markets, and estimates much wolfram was diverted via Shantou and Guangzhou; Japan used depreciated currency to attract raw materials, worsening inflation.
